32778-a-pushcart-at-the-curb:
John Dos Passos gathers poems of travel in this Doran volume of 1922, dedicated to Wright McCormick, who fell from a mountain in Mexico. His opening poem refuses the upholstered chariot and the shining limousine for a pushcart instead.

The cart is crazy and creaking, slung on shaky patchwork wheels, jolting over cobblestones with Spanish oranges, Smyrna figs, and fly-specked apples. Sections follow winter in Castile, nights at Bassano, third-class carriages, the Quai de la Tournelle, foreign travel, and phases of the moon. Bordeaux streets, blind musicians, Madrid coffee grinders, and an Asolo festival to Cypris fill the lading.
43494-congregationalism-in-the-court-sub:
Congregationalism in the Court Suburb, by John Stoughton, formerly minister of Kensington Chapel, was published in London in 1883 by Hodder and Stoughton. Stoughton prepared the sketch at the request of the chapel's present minister and deacons, and inscribed it to them. His introduction paints Kensington as it stood at the close of the last century, when the first Nonconformist church there was formed.

Stoughton warns that parish and village must be kept apart in the mind. The parish bounds stand unaltered, yet its contents have changed beyond knowing. He quotes a survey of 1795: near nineteen hundred acres, half of them pasture meadow, with arable land, market gardens, and nursery grounds. Against that rural ground he sets the built suburb of his own day, and tells how the chapel grew within it.
49579-little-lord-fauntleroy-abridged-fu:
Little Lord Fauntleroy is a cut school form of the famed tale by Frances Hodgson Burnett, made for the class room in a far tongue. It is past seventy of a set of school books in two tongues. This is its past form but six, out at a book town in nineteen four. The cut was made by a guide of that land past the leave of the first house.

Its front note, in that tongue, tells the task was to cut the tale so a class could end it in one school term. All parts not firm needs of the tale were struck out, and the rest cut as far as clear sense let. The whole came to past a third of its first size with the thread whole. Foot notes gloss the words of the new world for young hands of that land.
55642-the-sacred-herb:
Fergus Hume wrote The Sacred Herb, issued in New York in January 1908. Hume was known for The Mystery of a Hansom Cab and other tales. The tale opens with Lord Prelice, bored to despair on a bright summer morning in London. Born to a title, good looks, health, and an income well into five figures, he should be happy.

All play and no work has left him stale, and even a fine breakfast bores him. He reads the papers from habit and wonders how to fill the next day. His aunt, Lady Sophia, finds him in that mood. Contents promise a trial, a paper-cutter, a masked ball, and a startling discovery. Doctor Horace, Mrs Rover, and a place called Lanwin Grange all play parts.
56029-erb:
Erb is a novel by Pett Ridge, issued at New York in 1902. Its first chapter opens at an open air meeting. A red faced man on a chair shouts that his time is used up. Another speaker is here to address you, he cries. He means our friend Barnes, better known perhaps to all of you as Erb.

The crescent crowd growls its approval, and a round faced young man at the chair's side looks modestly at the sky. Erb hails from Bermondsey, the chairman says, where he holds a certain weight. In spite of his youth he is known as a real power in the labour world. He hits straight from the shoulder, and fears neither friend nor foe. Ridge was the comic laureate of London's working poor, and Erb is his labour hero.
britannica-1911-herb: Herb, from the Latin herba, grass or food for cattle, is the botanical name for plants whose stem dies back each year. Such stems die in whole or down to the root. They do not turn woody and lasting, as in shrubs or trees, and the plants are also called herbaceous. The word also covers plants prized for healing uses. Others serve for flavouring or garnishing food, and some for perfumes. This brief definition sits inside a larger hosted file that also holds neighbouring entries.
britannica-1911-rhubarb:
Rhubarb is a plant article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a name that covers both a drug and a vegetable. The drug is very old. It is described in a Chinese herbal said to date from 2700 before Christ. The name seems to be a worn form of a Latin phrase for a foreign root.

In the fourteenth century the drug reached Europe by way of India, the Persian Gulf, and Alexandria. That stock was called East Indian rhubarb. Other stock came through Persia and Syria and was sold as Turkey rhubarb. After 1653, when China let Russia trade at her borders, Chinese rhubarb came chiefly through Moscow. In 1704 that trade became a Russian crown monopoly. The entry follows a prized root along the trade roads of three continents.
doe-osti-2574166-modular-processing-of-f:
Final technical report DE-FE0031870, from the University of Colorado Boulder under Alan W. Weimer with Mija Hubler and partner Forge Nano, covers May 2020 to March 2025. The project turns flare gas, natural gas now burned off at wells, into carbon nanoproducts for concrete. A modular reactor is meant to travel to the gas instead of waiting for pipelines.

At lab scale, a fluidized bed reactor ran chemical vapor deposition over nickel catalysts laid on silica fume by atomic layer deposition. Tuning the catalyst particles lifted carbon yield to 31.8 percent by weight, with filaments confirmed under the microscope. A pilot unit was then built for continuous runs at up to one kilogram of carbon per hour, at 675 to 800 degrees Celsius. A missing downfeed tube capped its yield in early tests. Pricing analysis put the product's break-even below seven dollars per kilogram.
doe-osti-2999052-measurement-of-local-el:
Benedikt Geiger's final report for University of Wisconsin award DE-FG02-89ER53296 closes a fusion diagnostics project that ran from 1989 to 2024. Raymond Fonck led it until 2019, then Geiger took over. The goal was instruments that can measure turbulence in magnetically confined plasmas: tiny, fast swings in density, temperature, flow and electric field that leak heat from fusion fuel.

Four diagnostic lines came out of the decades of work. Beam-emission spectroscopy tracked local density turbulence at high speed. Alpha-CHERS probed how well fusion-born alpha particles stay confined. A fast charge-exchange system measured ion temperature and plasma rotation. Spatial heterodyne spectroscopy read local electric and magnetic fields at the plasma edge in under a millisecond. Together these tools let modellers test gyrokinetic turbulence codes against real data, and pinned down effects such as zonal flows and trapped electron modes.
nasa-tm-19640023710-long-period-contribu:
T. L. Felsentreger and W. J. Wickless of Goddard wrote this paper in August 1964. It treats slow drifts in satellite orbits caused by Earth's uneven gravity. Those uneven pulls are summed up as zonal harmonics in the title. The seventh, ninth, and eleventh harmonics are its focus.

Catalog notes say the paper gives formulas for long-period terms. Such terms build up slowly over many orbits of a satellite. Ignoring them makes predicted positions wander off over time. Higher harmonics refine the gravity map beyond the main bulge terms. The work is pure orbit bookkeeping, the kind of math that kept early satellite tracking honest.
nasa-tm-19670006712-ground-test-faciliti:
John R. Esterly, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, gave this lecture at the University of Tennessee Space Institute in Tullahoma on January 31, 1967. It formed one of thirty-two lectures in a two-week course on aerospace test facilities. Esterly's subject is the ground facilities needed to develop and evaluate advanced airbreathing engines, the jet engines that power aircraft.

Esterly traces how flight progress has always followed engine progress, from early gasoline engines to the Wright brothers and Glenn Curtiss. As engines and aircraft grew more complex, he argues, ground test facilities took on a central support role. Good facilities let engineers solve altitude and high-speed problems on the ground. That avoids flight tests that would otherwise be costly, hazardous, and slow.
nasa-tm-19680001473-decontamination-tech:
Francis N. LeDoux, at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, explains how to clean a spacecraft bound for the Moon, in October 1966. The worry is biological: Earth microbes riding along could confuse the search for lunar life. Every lunar orbiter or lander had to be made biologically clean.

NASA's quarantine office ruled that full sterilization was not required for the Moon. The Moon's harsh surface would keep any contamination local, the office reasoned. Still, viable organisms had to be cut to a low level before launch. LeDoux developed decontamination methods for the AIMP spacecraft series. A test program first checked that parts could survive the cleaning chemicals.
